units.source: ASARAMEL
units.target: ASARAMEL

units.source: a-sar'-a-mel (Asaramel or Saramel): A name of uncertain origin occurring in 1 Macc 14:28, in the inscription set up in memory of Simon and the Maccabean family. "On the eighteenth day of Elul, in the hundred and seventy and second year, and this is the third year of Simon the high priest, in Asaramel, in a great congregation of priests and people and princes of the nation, and of the elders of the country," etc. The phrase "in Asaramel" has been taken as referring to a place, and as the name of a title of Simon. Ewald and others take it to be the equivalent of ba-chatsar `am 'el, "in the court of the people of God." Another reading is "in Saramel." The majority prefer to take the phrase as a title of Simon; the original phrase is then taken to have been wesar `am 'el, "and prince of the people of God," i.e. ethnarch. If the translator mistook the waw (w) for beth (b) and read 'en, he might have left the phrase untranslated because he supposed it to be the name of a place. Schurer disposes of the en by taking it as a corruption of segen = ceghen, which is equivalent to the Greek strategos (GVI, I, 197, note 17).
units.target: a-sar'-a-mel (Asaramel ou Saramel) : Nom d'origine incertaine figurant en 1 Maccabées 14:28 dans l'inscription commémorant Simon et la famille des Maccabées : « Le dix-huitième jour du mois d'Éloul, en la cent soixante-douzième année, troisième année de Simon grand prêtre, à Asaramel, dans une grande assemblée de prêtres, de peuple, de princes de la nation et d'anciens du pays », etc. L'expression « à Asaramel » a été interprétée soit comme un lieu, soit comme un titre de Simon. Ewald et d'autres la comprennent comme l'équivalent de ba-chatsar `am 'el, « dans la cour du peuple de Dieu ». Une autre lecture donne « à Saramel ». La majorité préfère y voir un titre de Simon ; l'expression originale serait wesar `am 'el, « et prince du peuple de Dieu », autrement dit ethnarque. Si le traducteur confondit waw (w) et beth (b) et lut 'en, il aurait pu laisser la formule sans traduction, la croyant un nom de lieu. Schürer élimine en en le considérant comme une corruption de segen ou ceghen, équivalant au grec strategos (GVI, I, p. 197, note 17).

units.source: ASH (1)
units.target: FRÊNE (1)

units.source: ash ('oren; the Revised Version (British and American) FIR-TREE; the Revised Version, margin Ash): A maker of idols "planteth a fir- tree (margin, "ash"), and the rain doth nourish it" (
units.target: ash ('oren ; « sapin » dans la Revised Version britannique et américaine, « frêne » en note) : Un fabricant d'idoles « plante un sapin » (en note : « frêne ») « et la pluie le fait croître » (

units.source: ). It is a suggestion as old as Luther that the final letter "n", was originally a "z", and that the word should be 'erez, "cedar"; the chief objection is that cedar occurs just before in the same verse. The word 'oren seems to be connected with the Assyrian irin, meaning fir or cedar or allied tree. "Fir" has support from the Septuagint and from the rabbis. Post (HDB) suggests as probable the stone pine, Pinus pinea, which has been extensively planted round Beirut and unlike most planted trees flourishes without artificial watering--"the rain doth nourish it."
units.target: ). Depuis Luther, certains suggèrent que le « n » final était autrefois « z » et qu'il faudrait lire 'erez, « cèdre » ; objection principale : le cèdre est déjà nommé juste avant, dans le même verset. 'Oren semble apparenté à l'assyrien irin, « sapin », « cèdre » ou arbre voisin. La lecture « sapin » est soutenue par la Septante et les rabbins. Post (HDB) propose le pin parasol Pinus pinea, abondamment planté autour de Beyrouth, capable contrairement à bien d'autres arbres cultivés de prospérer sans arrosage artificiel : « la pluie le fait croître ».

units.source: The translation "ash" was probably suggested by the fanciful resemblance of the Hebrew 'oren and the Latin ornus, the manna ash of Europe. Three varieties of ash flourish in Syria, Fraxinus ornus, F. excelsior and F. oxycarpa. The last mentioned, which is common in parts of North Palestine, being a large tree some 30 to 40 ft. high, might suit the context were there anything philological to support the idea.
units.target: La traduction « frêne » vient probablement d'un rapprochement fantaisiste entre l'hébreu 'oren et le latin ornus, nom du frêne à manne d'Europe. Trois variétés de frênes poussent en Syrie : Fraxinus ornus, F. excelsior et F. oxycarpa. La dernière, fréquente dans certaines régions du nord de la Palestine, atteint neuf à douze mètres et pourrait convenir au contexte s'il existait un appui philologique.

units.source: ask (sha'al "to inquire," "to seek for counsel," "to demand"): It is the word commonly used in the Old Testament and is equivalent to eperotao, "to request," used in the New Testament. It does not imply any inferiority on the part of the person asking (

units.source: ). It is the Son who is bidden to ask, and therefore the word expresses the request of an equal. It has also the meaning "to inquire": "Wherefore .... ask after my name?" (
units.target: ) : le Fils est invité à demander, ce qui exprime la requête d'un égal. Le mot signifie aussi « interroger » : « Pourquoi demandes-tu mon nom ? » (

units.source: ) signifying, "Surely you must know who I am." "Ye shall ask me no question" (
units.target: ), soit « Tu dois certainement savoir qui je suis ». « Vous ne m'interrogerez plus » (

units.source: ), i.e. "about the true meaning of My words, for all will then be clear to you" (Dummelow). aiteo, is the word commonly used with reference to prayer. It means "to ask," "to implore," and presents the petitioner as an inferior asking from a superior (
units.target: ) signifie, selon Dummelow, « sur le vrai sens de mes paroles, car tout sera clair pour vous ». Aiteo est habituellement employé pour la prière. Il signifie « demander », « supplier », présentant le demandeur comme inférieur à celui qui reçoit la requête (

units.source: , and in many other places). It is not, however, asking in the sense of the word beg, but rather that of a child making request of its father. The petitioner asks both because of his need and of the assurance that he is welcome. He is assured before he asks that the petition will be granted, if he asks in accordance with God's will (1
units.target: et bien d'autres passages). Il ne s'agit pourtant pas de mendier, mais de demander comme un enfant à son père. Le croyant prie en raison de son besoin et de sa certitude d'être bienvenu. Il sait avant de demander que sa requête sera accordée si elle est conforme à la volonté de Dieu (1

units.source: ). Moreover the Spirit leads us to such asking in that He reveals our need and the goodness of God to us. See

units.source: Used with beautiful and comforting significance of death (koimaomai, "to put to sleep").
units.target: Employé avec une signification belle et consolante pour désigner la mort (koimaomai, « faire dormir »).

units.source: Sleep implies a subsequent waking, and as a symbol of death implies continued and conscious life beyond the grave. In the presence of death no truth has been so sustaining to Christian faith as this. It is the distinct product of Christ's resurrection. Paul speaks of departed believers as having "fallen asleep in Christ" (
units.target: Le sommeil implique un réveil ultérieur et, comme symbole de la mort, suggère une vie continue et consciente au-delà de la tombe. Face à la mort, aucune vérité n'a, selon cette notice, autant soutenu la foi chrétienne. Elle est un fruit distinct de la résurrection du Christ. Paul dit des croyants décédés qu'ils « se sont endormis en Christ » (

units.source: ); as proof of the soul's immortality he terms the risen Christ "the first- fruits of them that are asleep." Lazarus and Stephen, at death, are said to have "fallen asleep" (
units.target: ) ; pour témoigner de l'immortalité de l'âme, il appelle le Christ ressuscité « prémices de ceux qui se sont endormis ». Il est dit de Lazare et d'Étienne qu'ils « s'endormirent » à leur mort (

units.source: ); so of David and the ancient patriarchs (
units.target: ) ; de même de David et des anciens patriarches (

units.source: ). The most beautiful description of death in human language and literature is Paul's characterization of the dead as "them also which sleep in Jesus" (
units.target: ). La plus belle description de la mort dans la langue et la littérature humaines serait, selon l'auteur, la formule par laquelle Paul désigne les morts comme « ceux qui dorment en Jésus » (

units.source: the King James Version). This blessed hope has wrought itself permanently into the life and creed and hymnology of the Christian church, as in the hymn often used with such comforting effect at the burial service of believers: "Asleep in Jesus! blessed sleep!"

units.source: az-mo-de'-us ('ashmedhai; Asmodaios): An evil spirit first mentioned in Tobit 3:8. Older etymologists derived the name from the Hebrew verb shamadh, "destroy"; but it is now generally held to be associated with Zoroastrianism, with which the Jews became acquainted during the exile, and by which later Jewish views on the spirit-world were greatly influenced. It is now held to be the equivalent of the Persian Aeshma-Deva, the spirit of concupiscence. The spirit is at times reckoned as the equal in power of "Abaddon" (
units.target: az-mo-de'-us ('ashmedhai ; Asmodaios) : Esprit mauvais mentionné d'abord dans Tobie 3:8. Les anciens étymologistes faisaient dériver son nom du verbe hébreu shamadh, « détruire ». On l'associe plus généralement au zoroastrisme, que les Juifs découvrirent pendant l'exil et qui influença fortement les conceptions juives ultérieures du monde des esprits. Il serait l'équivalent du persan Aeshma-Deva, esprit de concupiscence. On lui attribue parfois un pouvoir comparable à celui d'« Abaddon » (

units.source: ) and of "Apollyon" (
units.target: ) ou d'« Apollyon » (

units.source: ), and in Tobit is represented as loving Sara, only daughter of Raguel of Ecbatana, and as causing the death on the bridal night of seven husbands who had in succession married her. His power was broken by the young Tobias acting on the advice of the angel Raphael (Tobit 6:15). He burnt on the "ashes of incense" the heart and liver of a fish which he caught in the Tigris. "But when the devil smelled the smell, he fled into the uppermost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him" (Tobit 8:3). Milton refers to the incident in Paradise Lost, 4, 168-71, founding on Jewish demonology and the "loves of the angels" (
units.target: ). Dans Tobie, il aime Sara, fille unique de Ragouël d'Ecbatane, et cause la mort, pendant la nuit de noces, de sept hommes qu'elle avait successivement épousés. Sa puissance fut brisée par le jeune Tobias, sur le conseil de l'ange Raphaël (Tobie 6:15). Tobias brûla sur les « cendres de l'encens » le cœur et le foie d'un poisson qu'il avait pris dans le Tigre. « Mais lorsque le diable sentit cette odeur, il s'enfuit dans les régions les plus reculées de l'Égypte, et l'ange l'enchaîna » (Tobie 8:3). Milton évoque cet épisode dans Le Paradis perdu (IV, 168–171), en s'appuyant sur la démonologie juive et les « amours des anges » (

units.source: a-sas'-inz (sicarioi; the King James Version murderers): Josephus (BJ, II, xiii, 3, xvii) relates that "there sprang up in Jerusalem a class of robbers called Sicarii, who slew men in the daytime, and in the midst of the city. This they did chiefly when they mingled with the populace at the festivals, and, hiding short daggers in their garments, stabbed with them those that were their enemies. The first to be assassinated by them was Jonathan the high priest, and after him many were slain daily" (see also Ant, XX, viii, 6, ix). The name is derived from Latin sica, "a dagger." The sicarioi were implacable in their hatred to Rome and to those Jews who were suspected of leaning toward Rome. They took a leading part in the Jewish rebellion and in the disturbance previous to it, and also in the faction quarrels during the war. After the war they continued their nefarious practices in Egypt and Cyrene whither they had fled. Lysias mistook Paul for `the Egyptian who .... led out into the wilderness the 4,000 men of the sicarioi' (
units.target: a-sas'-inz (sicarioi, « meurtriers » dans la King James Version) : Josèphe (Guerre des Juifs, II, xiii, 3 ; xvii) raconte qu'« apparut à Jérusalem une catégorie de brigands appelés Sicaires, qui tuaient en plein jour, au milieu de la ville. Ils agissaient surtout en se mêlant à la foule lors des fêtes et, cachant de courts poignards dans leurs vêtements, frappaient leurs ennemis. Le premier qu'ils assassinèrent fut Jonathan, grand prêtre ; ensuite, beaucoup furent tués chaque jour » (voir aussi Antiquités judaïques, XX, viii, 6, ix). Le nom dérive du latin sica, « poignard ». Les sicarioi vouaient une haine implacable à Rome et aux Juifs soupçonnés d'être favorables aux Romains. Ils jouèrent un rôle majeur dans la révolte juive, dans les troubles qui la précédèrent et les luttes de factions pendant la guerre. Après celle-ci, ils poursuivirent leurs activités criminelles en Égypte et à Cyrène, où ils s'étaient réfugiés. Lysias confondit Paul avec « l'Égyptien qui […] avait conduit au désert quatre mille sicaires » (

a-sem'-bliz, (ba`ale 'acuppoth,

): the American Revised Version, margin "collectors of sentences," thus Qimchi, Grotius and others. This has been variously interpreted. Tyler translates "editors of collections." Klienert renders "protectors of the treasure- chambers," 'acuppoth being considered equivalent to the 'acuppim of
(see
ASUPPIM
). The proverbs are like nails guarding the sacred storehouse, the book closing with this warning against touching the collection (compare
). Delitzsch translates "like fastened nails which are put together in collections." "As ba`ale berith (
) signifies `the confederates,' ba`ale shebhu`ah (

) `the sworn,' and the frequently occurring ba`ale ha-`ir `the citizens': so ba`ale 'acuppoth means, the possessors of assemblies and of the assembled themselves, or the possessors of collections and of things collected. Thus ba`ale 'acuppoth will be a designation of the `words of the wise' (as in shalishim, "choice men" = choice proverbs,
, in a certain measure personified), as of those which form or constitute collections and which stand together in order and rank" ("Eccl," English translation, 434).

The Jerusalem Talmud takes 'acuppoth as the Sanhedrin. On the whole it is better to interpret the phrase "persons skilled in collections" of wise sayings, grouped in a compact whole (compare Wright, Eccl, 102).
S. F. Hunter
ASSEMBLY
a-sem'-bli (qahal; ekklesia): The common term for a meeting of the people called together by a crier. It has reference therefore to any gathering of the people called for any purpose whatsoever (
the King James Version;
the King James Version;
). The solemn assemblies of the Jews were their feasts or religious gatherings of any kind (
). The word paneguris, "a general festal assembly" (

), is transferred from the congregation of the people of Israel to the Christian church of which the congregation of Israel was a figure. In the same passage, ekklesia has the sense of calling, summoning. In classical Greek ekklesia was the name for the body of free citizens summoned by a herald. In this sense the church calls all the world to become identified with it. It denotes the whole body of believers, all who are called. Or it may refer to a particular congregation or local church (sunagoge, "synagogue"

ASTONISHED; ASTONIED

as-ton'-isht, as-ton'-id (shamem, "astonished," the root idea being "silent," i.e. struck dumb with amazement; ekplessomai, "to be struck with astonishment," as if by a blow or a shock; existemi, "to amaze," "to throw into wonderment"; thambeomai, "to astonish" to the point of fright): The state of being surprised, startled, stunned by some exceptional wonder, some overwhelming event or miracle, as e.g. Nebuchadnezzar's amazement at the miracle in the burning fiery furnace (
) (tewah, "astonished"); of the passer-by at the desolation of Babylon (
). The personality, teaching and works of Jesus were so wonderful, Divine, supernatural, as to awaken emotions of surprise and awe never before known in the presence of man.
The people "were astonished out of measure" at His doctrine (
the King James Version); "astonished with a great astonishment" at His raising the dead (
the King James Version). The gift of the Holy Ghost to the Gentiles was in like manner a source of astonishment to those Jews who believed through the power of Peter's preaching (
the King James Version). The miracle of regeneration today, which renews and transforms debased and fallen men into saints, makes the same impression on an observing world.
Dwight M. Pratt
ASYLUM

a-si'-lum: The custom of fleeing to specially sacred places to obtain the protection of a deity is found all over the world (Post, Grundriss, II, 252 ff). In ancient Israel we meet with it in two forms--the asylum of the altar and the asylum of the cities of refuge. The altar at the House of God was a place to which persons in danger fled for protection (
). It had horns and must not be confused with the altars of earth or stone that were used for lay sacrifices. See
ALTAR
SANCTUARY
provides that a murderer is to be taken from the altar to be put to death. The law of the cities of refuge proceeds upon a somewhat different principle. Its objects are
(1) to shield a homicide from the avenger of blood until trial, and
(2) to provide a refuge for the manslayer who has not been guilty of murder. There is one reference to the institution in the history of the kingdom (
). For the legal and geographical information, see
CITIES OF REFUGE
HOMICIDE
Harold M. Wiener
ATARGATIS
a-tar'-ga-tis (Atargatis; the Revised Version (British and American) wrongly
ATERGATIS

Is stated in 2 Macc 12:26 to have been worshipped at Karnion, the Ashtaroth-Karnaim of the Old Testament (compare Ant, XII, viii, 4). The name is found on coins of Membij as `atar-`atah, where `Atar (i. e. Ashtoreth) is identified with the goddess `Atah, whose name is sometimes written `Ati. or `Atah or `Ati was also worshipped at Palmyra, and (according to Melito) in Adiabene.

The compound Atargatis, often corrupted by the Greeks into Derketo, had her chief temples at Membij (Hierapolis) and Ashkelon where she was represented with the body of a woman and the tail of a fish, fish being sacred to her. Herodotus made her the Aphrodite Urania of the Greeks. `Ati may have been originally a Hittite goddess with whom the Assyrian Ishtar (`Atar) came afterward to be identified tory of the kingdom (
). For the legal and geographical information, see
CITIES OF REFUGE
HOMICIDE
A. H. Sayce

ATTIRE; DYED ATTIRE

a-tir': "Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire?" asks the prophet Jeremiah in hot remonstrance against Israel's unfaithfulness. "Yet," saith Yahweh, "my people have forgotten me" (2:32). "And I saw that she was defiled," cries Ezekiel against Jerusalem; "she saw men ... girded with girdles upon their loins, with flowing turbans [AV exceeding in dyed attire] upon their heads, ..... after the likeness of the Babylonians in Chaldea, .... and .... she doted upon them .... "(
). "And, behold, there met him," says the author of Pr (
) in his description of the "strange woman," that "lieth in wait at every street corner," "a woman with the attire of a harlot, and wily of heart," whose "house is the way to Sheol" (

). These passages show how diversely and elastically the term "attire" was used among the Hebrews. The numerous synonyms for "dress," "attire," "apparel," "clothes," "raiment," "garment," etc., found in English Versions of the Bible, reflect a similar wealth of nomenclature in the original Hebrew and Greek; but the lack of exactness and consistency in the renderings of translators makes the identification of the various articles of dress referred to very difficult, sometimes impossible. See
DRESS
George B. Eager
